comment: Implementation tracker for the design bible (design/index.html). Edit this file and the page follows: it reads the tracker live (npm run dev, then /design/). Status is one of: done, building, planned, idea. Keep `files` to the main places a feature lives so a future session can jump straight there.

features.title: Zone recipes generate the island
features.notes: Coastline, bays, sea cliffs, rolling hills, the Windspire with a ledge path cut along its contour lines, a quarry pit, flattened town ground, graded roads, surfaces. Same seed, same island.

features.title: Emberholm, the starter isle
features.notes: Lanternwick and its docks, Barleybrook Fields, Hearthside Rise, Windspire, Westwatch (land route), Gullrock (sea route), Thornwood, Stonebreak Quarry, Slime Meadow, Sunscale Strand; 12 townsfolk.

features.title: Open-world renderer
features.notes: Chunked terrain drawn from the physics grid (same triangle split, so feet sit on the drawn ground), depth-tinted sea with shoreline foam, sky dome and clouds, chunk-culled trees, a grass ring that follows you, the world tree on the horizon.

features.title: Buildings, props and colliders from data
features.notes: Footprints, colliders (box, walls with a doorway, posts) and walkable decks (piers, the glider launch) come from shared/structures.json.

features.title: Procedural models for every building, vehicle, crop and prop
features.notes: Low-poly toon models built in code to the data's exact footprints and anchors: 20 structures (the cottage in 5 build stages), 6 vehicles, 2 mounts, 2 gliders, 9 packs, 6 crops in 4 stages, 3 kinds of livestock (young and grown), 12 villagers and 8 props. Merged per model for few draw calls; tests check wheels, waterlines, seat heights and the cottage doorway.

features.title: Day and night
features.notes: A 30-minute day: the sun rises in the east, crosses the south and sets in the west; gold at dawn and dusk; moonlit blue nights with stars and lit windows; the sea and fog follow. The HUD shows the hour.

features.title: More zones and a sea between continents
features.notes: Zone streaming, a second continent, a contested open sea and an island outpost that pays best and is hardest to reach.

features.title: Terrain level of detail
features.notes: Coarser chunks in the distance if draw cost grows with more zones.

features.title: Walking over terrain
features.notes: Feet follow the ground; slopes steeper than 46 degrees and ledges over 0.45 m block you; walking off a ledge drops you; standing on a cliff face slides you off. The Windspire ledge path is tested to be climbable on foot, bottom to top.

features.title: Wading and swimming
features.notes: Shallow water slows you; deep water swims you at the surface (sprint to swim faster); walk out where it shallows, or jump at a dock edge to haul yourself out.

features.title: Gliders
features.notes: Jump, double jump, jump again to open; steer toward the stick; sprint to dive, crouch to flare (speed shed in a flare comes back as height). Wayfarer and Swiftwing. Cannot open with a pack on.

features.title: Rising air
features.notes: Updraft columns lift an open glider; visible as spiralling wisps at the Windspire's foot.

features.title: Glider gusts
features.notes: F in flight gives a burst of speed and lift on a cooldown (Wayfarer 30 s, Swiftwing 16 s), so you can claw back height or stretch a glide. Being knocked out of the air when hit is still to come.

features.title: Traversal on the server
features.notes: The server decides where everyone is. tests/conformance/terrain.test.ts bakes the whole generated island (ground, surfaces, cleared cells, trees and rocks, walls and decks) into crates/engine/data/emberholm.zone and checks it is current; crates/engine/src/open ports the colliders, walking over hills and cliffs, wading, swimming and gliding (traverse.ts), and runs each player's key presses through them. The browser predicts its own player with the TypeScript and corrects to the server's answer; tests/conformance/world.test.ts compares the two frame by frame.

features.title: Wheeled driving model
features.notes: Each vehicle keeps its own world velocity and only grips sideways, so handbrake turns slide; road vs offroad caps, sand drag, slopes pull, can leave the ground and land; trees, rocks and walls stop you.

features.title: Farm Cart, Roadster, Hauler
features.notes: 4, 1 and 8 pack slots. The roadster boosts with Shift and drifts with Space.

features.title: Rowboat and Sloop
features.notes: Boats run aground in water shallower than their draft. The sloop's W/S trims the sail; speed follows the angle to the wind.

features.title: Donkey and Horse
features.notes: R calls and rides your mount. Only the donkey carries a pack (at pack pace); the horse gallops with Shift.

features.title: Summon, board, cargo
features.notes: Deeds summon vehicles (boats at the nearest deep water). Walk to the seat to drive, to the bed to load or unload. Loaded vehicles cannot be sent home. A pack on your back keeps you out of a cart's or boat's seat: load it into the bed first (only a donkey carries you with one). Seats are where the model's seats are however the vehicle tilts, and the rider tilts with it; online, picking up, loading, unloading and getting in run at once in the browser and again on top of the server's answers until it has run them too.

features.title: Shipyards and the Merchant Cog
features.notes: Captain Ilsa sells the Merchant Cog Design (10s + 6 seals). Lay its keel on the Lanternwick slipway, then haul lumber bundles, iron crates and sailcloth (woven from flax at the Lanternwick bench) through four stages: keel, hull, deck, rigging. The hull visibly rises inside scaffolding; launching hands you the deed. 16 pack slots and a square sail.

features.title: Damage, repair and theft
features.notes: Boats now take hull damage in storms and break up (cargo floats, 90 s repair). Carts and cars still only take damage from hard landings; an owner’s mark, theft and salvage are still to come.

features.title: Riding along with friends
features.notes: Beside another player's cart, car or boat, F climbs into its free passenger seat ("Ride with <name>"), and you go wherever its owner drives; F gets you out beside it, and if it's sent home, wrecked or its owner leaves you're set down where it was. The channel seats passengers after everyone has moved (the player's host field says whose vehicle it is). Everyone else's vehicles are solid to you, ridden or not.

features.title: Walking the deck of a moving ship
features.notes: Standing and walking about on a sloop or cog while she sails, rather than only sitting in her seats.

features.title: Trade packs and material packs
features.notes: Four trade packs from the Lanternwick workbench; lumber bundles at Hob's sawhorse; stone blocks and iron crates at the stonecutter.

features.title: Carrying a pack
features.notes: On your back: 55% speed, no sprint, no double jump, no glider, lower jump. X drops it; F picks it up. Packs keep where they are in saves.

features.title: Trading posts, routes and prices
features.notes: Westwatch (land, ×1.0, 1 seal) and Gullrock (sea, ×1.5, 3 seals). Price = base × route × demand × freshness.

features.title: Demand and freshness
features.notes: Each sale drops that post's demand for that pack by 5% (floor 70%); it recovers 2% a minute up to 130%. Fresh packs earn +15% for 10 minutes, falling to -12% at 45.

features.title: Piracy
features.notes: Packs drop on death for anyone to take; a fence for stolen goods; the crafter keeps a cut when someone else delivers their pack.

features.title: Delayed payment with interest
features.notes: ArcheAge paid hours later with interest. Probably not worth the confusion; listed so the decision is explicit.

features.title: Scarecrow plots
features.notes: 8 × 8 m on open, level, grassy ground clear of roads, buildings and trees; up to three.

features.title: Crops and trees
features.notes: Sunroot, barley, flax, emberberry; apple trees fruit again and again; pines are felled for lumber.

features.title: Climate, watering and rain
features.notes: Out-of-climate crops grow at 70%; watering or rain speeds a stage by 25%.

features.title: Growth while you are away
features.notes: The world clock catches up on load (up to 12 hours), so crops ripen with the tab closed.

features.title: Gathering nodes
features.notes: Deadfall timber, stone, iron ore and wild herbs, each with a respawn; timber can turn up a thunderstruck log.

features.title: Livestock
features.notes: Chicks, lambs and calves from Sela, raised in plot cells: they grow up and then lay eggs, grow wool or give milk again and again, but only while fed on barley. Nothing dies of neglect; a hungry animal just waits. Eggs and milk go into a Farmhouse Hamper, wool into a Fleece Bale.

features.title: Larceny
features.notes: Crops on unprotected land can be taken; footprints, reports and a crime score.

features.title: Plots and blueprints
features.notes: Eight plots at Hearthside Rise; a Cottage Blueprint (3s + 3 seals) claims one. One house per settler for now.

features.title: Building in stages from hauled packs
features.notes: Foundation, frame, walls, roof: each needs its material packs delivered to the site and labor to finish.

features.title: A home that does something
features.notes: Solid walls and a doorway, a floor you stand on, a bed (labor ×3 while resting), a storage chest, property tax paid at the plot.

features.title: Neglect and plot recycling
features.notes: Unpaid tax leads to demolition after a grace period; freed plots go out by lottery, not to the fastest clicker.

features.title: More houses, furniture, friends helping
features.notes: Farmhouse, manor, aquafarm; placeable furniture; other players delivering packs to your site.

features.title: Coins, Charter Seals and labor
features.notes: Copper/silver/gold, seals from trade routes for land; labor regenerates 12 a minute online (6 offline), cap 1,000.

features.title: Vendors and crafters
features.notes: Mara (seeds, buys produce), Hob and Brenna (materials), Sela (mounts), Quill (land), Ysolde (gliders); Bertram and Ilsa build vehicles and boats from materials.

features.title: Player market and mail
features.notes: An auction house per region, mail with attachments.

features.title: Proficiencies
features.notes: Using labor in a trade levels it: lower labor costs, better yields, new recipes.

features.title: Starter questline
features.notes: Thirteen quests that teach farming, livestock, gliding, packing, contracts, carts, boats, building a house and building a ship, advanced by what you actually do. Anything you already did before taking a quest (a plot placed, a house raised, a ship launched) counts the moment you accept it.

features.title: Trade contracts
features.notes: Each trading post keeps two contracts on its board: so many packs of a kind within 25 minutes, for bonus seals and coin. Hold two at once; lapsed ones are replaced every ten minutes.

features.title: Open-world HUD
features.notes: In the Parchment & Timber look: your portrait and name, health and labor bars with the purse, a round minimap with zoom and quest marks, the clock and wind, a compass, the quest scroll with progress bars, menu buttons with their keys, the interaction prompt, toasts (small, at the bottom right under the quest tracker, clear of the bag and the ride readout), place banners and name plates.

features.title: Panels
features.notes: MMO windows docked at the sides, open while you walk (walking away from whoever you are talking to closes theirs): talking lists their quests and what they offer; quests have offer, progress and hand-in pages with objectives and rewards; the merchant has Buy, Sell and Buyback tabs beside your bag; workbench, storage, vehicles; a character window (P) with gear slots around a live picture of you, your combo damage and the skill points you have left; a two-pane quest log with milestones, where a quest can be abandoned or taken off the tracker; the map; settings (UI size, credits); the developer panel (backquote). Portraits come from the live scene; items, slots and rewards have tooltips.

features.title: Controller navigation in panels
features.notes: With a window open the D-pad or stick (or the arrow keys) moves a highlight over its buttons, A (Enter) presses the highlighted one and B (Escape) closes. On a controller an open window has the pad: you stand still and its D-pad no longer calls the mount or opens the map. The skill book and tree have their own cursor (View opens the book, a bumper turns to the tree).

features.title: Platform-fighter movement and weapons
features.notes: Run, sprint, crouch, slide, double jump; sword, club, staff, bow combos. Built before this session.

features.title: Skill tree and skill book
features.notes: The tree (N) is a chart of 226 nodes: four disciplines around you, each with its weapon next to you and its skills along a spine, and passives, notables and keystones between them, every one a modifier the rules already apply. You learn outward from what you know: click to plan the way to a node, Learn to spend the points, right-click to give one back (and whatever only it held up). The book (T) lists every weapon, ability and movement skill with its level, experience and numbers, and is where you equip a weapon and fill the hotbar and the Q / E keys. The fifteen old skills kept their places, links and costs, so saved builds still mean the same.

features.title: Battle server
features.notes: Rust server with 10,000 bots, prediction and lag compensation, conformance-tested against the browser rules. Built before this session.

features.title: Combat on terrain
features.notes: Arrows, meteors, damage numbers and hit sparks use the ground height under each creature. Swings measure how high you are from the ground under you (in the flat yard that is still just your height, as on the server), and on hills they only reach things whose feet are within 2 m of yours, so a slime down a cliff is out of reach. The slimes and the practice dummy on the hillside meadow (18 m up) can be fought with every weapon.

features.title: Life systems as a deterministic command model
features.notes: All open-world changes happen inside a sim step from queued commands (interact, buy, craft, summon...), which is the shape server requests will take.

features.title: Saving on the game server
features.notes: Your island is kept in Postgres with your character, written by the server from its own copy every 5 seconds and when you leave (a quick reload picks up exactly where you were). Time away still ripens crops, measured on the server. Only one window plays a character at a time; a newer one takes over. ?fresh starts over on the server. A saved island the server can't read is kept as it is and never written over. localStorage holds an island only for tests and bug-report replays (?world&test&load).

features.title: Accounts and sign-in
features.notes: Names and Argon2id password hashes in Postgres, a 30-day http-only session cookie the WebSocket carries too, wrong-password throttling, and a sign-in screen before Emberholm loads. One character per account for now, in its own table so accounts can hold more later. Development servers also sign in by name alone (?as=name), so tests and several test windows need no passwords; never on Railway.

features.title: One server, one port, ready for Railway
features.notes: The Rust server (axum) serves the account API and the open world's WebSocket on one port, plus the built game in production (the battlefield is a developer zone of the world since the refactor). The Dockerfile's last stage is what Railway deploys (railway.json); docker-compose.yml runs Postgres and the server for development, and Vite forwards /api and /ws to it so the browser sees one address either way.

features.title: Beta and production, with CI/CD
features.notes: Two protected branches: beta takes direct pushes, production only pull requests with CI passing. Every push and pull request typechecks and builds the client, runs the Rust tests, and plays the whole Playwright suite against a real server and Postgres (battlefield and conformance tests included). A passing push deploys to the Railway environment of the same name and waits for /api/health on the new deployment. Each environment has its own Postgres.

features.title: Open-world tests
features.notes: 25 Playwright tests drive terrain, swimming, gliding, gusts and updrafts, farming, livestock, packs, contracts, carts, cars, boats, storms, mounts, housing, the shipyard, quests, panels, saving and combat on the hills (arrows, and sword, club and staff swings at slimes and the dummy).

features.title: Bug reports recorded in play, fixed with /fix-bugs
features.notes: Press \ (or click both sticks) when something goes wrong: the game keeps the last 30 s (frames 4 a second, the player 10 times a second, every input, events, console and errors), takes a screenshot with the HUD, then records your voice (live transcript), the screen and the state until you press it again. The dev server saves it to bugs/; /fix-bugs in Claude Code reads it with tools/bugs.mjs, reproduces the bug on the saved island, fixes it and closes the report. Frames are encoded in a worker, so it costs no frame time.

features.title: Design bible drawn from the game's own modules
features.notes: design/index.html is the prose; design/bible.ts draws every table, chart, calculator and the map from the content modules, the rules' formulas (freshness, climate) and the terrain generator, and the tracker from this file. The dev server serves it at /design/. Nothing is generated or copied, so it is always current. tests/integration/design.spec.ts checks it draws without errors.

features.title: A world server
features.notes: The server plays Emberholm. Browsers send only key presses (60 a second, binary) and commands (talk, plant, buy, craft, summon, drive...); each channel's game on the server (crates/server/src/play/mod.rs, 20 ticks a second) runs them through the island's rules ported to Rust (crates/engine/src/open: ground, colliders, traversal; crates/engine/src/life: trade, farming, livestock, housing, shipyard, vehicles, quests, contracts, weather), the battlefield's combat, and the channel's own slimes, then tells each browser where it is, what its island holds, and what everyone else is doing. The browser predicts its own moves and vehicles with the TypeScript and corrects itself; tests/conformance/world.test.ts and tests/conformance/life.test.ts keep the two agreeing. Islands are one JSON document per character in Postgres, written only by the server. Phases: (1) accounts and islands on the server, (2) movement on the server, (3) life on the server, (4) one shared Emberholm in channels, (5) live on Railway: all done.

features.title: One shared Emberholm, in channels
features.notes: Channels are copies of the island, each home to up to 24 characters, who keep the one they were first given. Everyone in a channel sees everyone else (position, animation, glider, pack, vehicles and mounts, relayed about 20 times a second and drawn 100 ms behind with names over their heads) and everything each resident has built (houses, farms, ships on the slipway), which stays when they log off and is solid. A house plot belongs to whoever built on it first; the server keeps the claims. The developer panel is on in development and beta, off in production.

features.title: A camera that respects walls
features.notes: The camera pulls in instead of looking through buildings, which also makes walking into your cottage work.

features.title: Walls-down view indoors
features.notes: Step inside a finished house and its walls are cut to waist height, like a dollhouse, so you can see yourself, the bed, the chest and the hearth; the camera stops pulling in.

features.title: Weather and wind
features.notes: Rain showers every 7 to 13 minutes water every field; the wind wanders round the compass and drives the sloop.

features.title: Storms at sea
features.notes: In the rain, open water deeper than 5 m turns rough: the swell shoves boats about and wears down the hull (a rowboat in under a minute of full storm, a cog hardly at all). A boat that breaks up spills its cargo, which floats where she sank for you to swim out and recover; she is back after a 90-second repair.

features.title: Townsfolk with their own looks
features.notes: All twelve villagers have their own model and outfit that says their trade at a glance (the elder's robe and staff, Mara's basket, Ilsa's tricorn, Pell's top hat...). They breathe and look around, turn to face you when you come close, and gesture while you talk.

features.title: Slime pack fight
features.notes: Four sizes on a ladder (slimelet, slime, great slime, slime monarch), each its own kind with mass, health, scale and slam. Slimes leave you alone until you hit one. Then: the one you hit calls (if its gather is ready) and the pack within 14 m rushes to it; with two within 8 m it gathers for 2.5 s (green swirl, cast bar on its plate), pulling them in and growing to the size their mass reaches, at full health; a quarter of its health in damage breaks the cast and dazes it, and if the caller dies the nearest rallying slime takes over. Anything angry in range winds up, leaps and slams where you stood (red ring). A kill bursts into 3/5/7 slimelets on a 6 s fuse that run while you are close and huddle otherwise; two or more left reform one size up from what you killed. A lone survivor dissolves; no creature passes 40 alive, and home slimes respawn only within the starting mass. Brains are data with guarded transitions, interrupts and requests the world carries out, the same in TypeScript and Rust, compared pack by pack in ai-conformance.

features.title: A jointed hero, animated from scratch
features.notes: Knees, ankles, elbows, a neck, blinking eyes and a two-piece cape (23 joints). Every animation redone with two-bone IK: a gait whose planted feet stay put at any speed or heading (walk, jog, run, sprint, creep, carry, strafe, back off), heel-to-toe roll, leaning into turns; sword, club and staff swings as keyframes with a wind-up, the body leading the arm, footwork that steps with the lunge and two-handed grips, and the sword carried ready (blade up and forward) when running; a bow drawn to the chin, the arrow in front of the chest and the string following the hand; casts, guard, slide, rolls and flips in eight directions, hits that throw the body the way the blow shoves it, knock-downs. Travelling, the hero takes hold of the vehicle as it moves (vehicles.ts Holds): hands on the steering wheel's rim (the wheels turn, square on their columns and facing the driver) and on the oars' handles mid-stroke, thighs out over the seat's edge and feet on the footrest; on a horse the knees bend round its body to short stirrups; the glider bar sits ahead of the chin. The cape takes the wind from the way you go. Weapon trails are traced from the blade. The close-up hero eases between states, holds planted feet where they are and the way they point through turns and stops, stepping round one foot at a time when they get too far out, and draws frame counters between sim steps. The crowd bakes its clips from the same poses.

features.title: Weapons out for a fight, put away after
features.notes: The weapon comes out while an enemy is marked (soft lock counts) or for 1.5 s after a swing or cast, the combat stance's rule, and goes away 2.5 s after: drawn in 0.45 s, put away in 0.6 s, the drawing hand reaching to where it hangs and taking it over halfway, without a jump. Swinging, shooting, casting or guarding puts it in hand at once. On foot the sword and club hang at the right hip, the staff over the right shoulder and the bow high by the left; travelling, along the body (swimming, gliding), down the horse's side, back over the boat at the oars, across the lap in a seat. Other players' heroes go by what they're doing and keep it out 4 s; on the battlefield it's always out. Drawing only: no rules change.

features.title: Combat stance: strafing, backing off, dodging any way
features.notes: With an enemy marked, or for 1.5 s after a swing or cast, you keep facing where the camera looks: the stick strafes (85% speed) and backs off (65%), and dodges and double jumps go wherever you push without turning you; attacks and unaimed casts go off ahead. Sprinting turns and runs. A facing intent in the input (one byte on the wire: battlefield inputs are 16 bytes, open-world ones 10) and the same rule in TypeScript and Rust, checked frame by frame.

features.title: Parchment & Timber look
features.notes: Parchment panels in timber frames with brass trim and rivets, two bundled typefaces (TeX Gyre Pagella, Alegreya SC) and painted icons for every item, skill, place and the HUD's own (hearts, coins, menu buttons, quest marks): 135 of them, painted nine to a sheet with Gemini (tools/icons/paint.mjs, from tools/icons/catalog.mjs) and cut out by tools/icons/bake.mjs (npm run icons) as 128 px WebP. CREDITS.md and the Settings window name the sources.

features.title: A UI that scales with the window
features.notes: Laid out for a screen 1029 px tall and scaled to the window, so it keeps its size relative to the screen at any resolution; Settings has a UI size slider on top of that.

features.title: Skill points from quests and milestones
features.notes: No character levels: you start with 2 points (skills.startPoints) and every quest and milestone you finish gives more (rewards.skillPoints: 21 from the thirteen quests, 8 from the milestones). They are counted from the quests you have done rather than kept, so islands saved before they existed have theirs too. The server checks every build against them, and so does the browser; the training yard and the battlefield allow skills.points. The amounts stay as they are for now (decided 2026-11-04), to be retuned once the island has been played through.

features.title: Skills level by use
features.notes: Each weapon gains experience for every hit it lands, each ability for every cast, each movement skill for every use, and levels up along tuning.json skills.levels (ten levels). A level adds a little to what it does (damage, healing, quicker recovery), the island keeps the experience, and the server counts it online. A level-up says so and counts toward the Practised Hand milestone.

features.title: Milestones
features.notes: Quests with nobody to hand them to: they start when their prerequisites are done and finish the moment their steps are, each worth a skill point. Green Thumb (30 harvests), Sky Legs (two minutes gliding), Pack Mule (5 deliveries), Rancher (3 animals), Contract Hand (5 contracts), Wayfarer (every corner of the island), Slime Hunter (15 slimes) and Practised Hand (5 skill levels). The quest log has a part for them; the quest scroll leaves them out.

features.title: Abandoning a quest
features.notes: The quest log's Abandon (asked once more) takes a quest off your list with its progress, and its giver offers it again. Milestones and the quests that start by themselves can't be abandoned; one that handed you something to start with takes it back, and can't be abandoned once you've used it. Both rules (abandon, quests.rs).

features.title: Buyback
features.notes: A merchant holds what you sold them, at what they paid (the last twelve sales), and sells it back from the stall's Buyback tab until you walk 12 m off. Both rules (state.buyback, trade.rs).

features.title: Title screen, sign-in and character select
features.notes: The game opens on a dusk title scene (drawn by index.html before the code arrives) with a loading bar fed by real steps; sign-in, account creation and the character select screen sit on it. An account holds up to six characters, each with its own island; the select screen shows the chosen hero live in 3D, with Enter World, Create Character and Delete Character (type the name). Characters and Settings > Exit to Character Select go back to it from the world.

features.title: Riding out a server update
features.notes: A stopping server (a deploy) tells every player it is updating, saves every island, then closes with 1012. The page freezes the world under a "Ruina Is Being Updated" card, reconnects by itself, and reloads straight back into the world with the same character when a new build or protocol is out. A dropped connection freezes the same way. railway.json gives the old server 20 s to do it.

features.title: Animation library: review animations and send Claude the fixes
features.notes: /dev/library.html shows every animated thing: the hero (each film in scenarios.ts, in the made body or the box one, any weapon), slimes in every size (as jelly or boxes), the crowd's far-away bodies, the farm animals, the twelve townsfolk and the mounts. Pick one, then an animation; play it at any speed, step it a frame at a time, scrub, loop a stretch, look from any side, with its skeleton, onion skins and the paths of its hands and feet. The timeline shows what the rules have the body doing when (a swing's wind-up, strike and recovery, the air, a landing). Notes go on the whole animation, a stretch of frames or one frame; on a frame you can move the bones (turn a joint, or take a hand or a foot and bend the limb to reach it) and keep the corrected pose with a picture of before and after. Create Prompt turns the open notes into one prompt for Claude: what moves each body and where, every note with the rules' state on its frames, and for corrected poses the bones' turns in degrees, where the hands and feet went in centimetres, and the pictures. The notes are kept by the dev server in reviews/animations/ (tools/animReviews.ts), so they outlive the reload a code change brings; corrected poses then show as green ghosts on their frames, with how close the animation now comes. tests/integration/library-review.spec.ts measures every correction against the code (REVIEW=.../review.json), and the animation-review skill says how to work through a review.

features.title: Stamina and MP
features.notes: Every fighter has health, MP and stamina (and labor on the island). Dodge Roll and Backstep cost stamina instead of a cooldown; Healing Circle and Meteor cost MP, paid when the cast goes off. Values in shared/tuning.json (stamina, mp, staminaCost, mpCost). Shown beside your portrait, over the hotbar off the island, and on the Q and E slots, which shade when you can not afford them.

features.title: Walking onto platforms
features.notes: Decks (the glider launch, piers) are walked up onto as high as ground.deckStep, and one you can neither step onto nor pass under is solid from the side, so you no longer walk under the launch deck. The body eases up over the step.

features.title: Monsters online, smooth and readable
features.notes: Online, monsters are drawn interpolated at the moment other players are (they moved in 20 Hz jumps); warning circles lie on the hills (they were drawn at sea level, under the ground); a hit sparks, shakes, pauses and flashes the slime the moment your blade connects, with the server's number following; anyone's hit flashes the monster. Slimes can be soft-locked online.

features.title: An overhead chop in the air
features.notes: A sword swung in the air raises the blade straight up overhead, then chops down in front, playing through if you land halfway.

features.title: Item menus: click, double-click, right-click
features.notes: In the bag a click picks an item out, a double-click does its main thing (place the scarecrow, plant, equip, summon; sell at a merchant, store at your chest) and a right-click opens a menu of what can be done with it now; A and Y on a controller. The merchant's goods have menus too.

features.title: The UI design system
features.notes: design/ui.html: the look, the writing rules (labels in Title Case, sentences in sentence case: src/ui/theme/text.ts), where everything sits on screen, every component drawn with the game's own styles, and how items answer the mouse and a controller. tests/integration/ui.spec.ts holds the open windows to the rules.

features.title: Auto-run and travel by road
features.notes: H or Num Lock (a quick click of the left stick at rest) runs you on where the camera looks; in a cart or boat it holds the throttle. A click on the big map marks a place and follows the roads there (the road network joins where roads meet and across the town square), on foot, on a mount or in a cart; a place a few steps off the road is walked to, a far one gets you as near as the road goes. Your own movement, mounting, water or getting stuck stops it.

features.title: One time of day and weather for everyone
features.notes: Online the sky, the HUD clock, the rain and the wind follow the server's clock (the welcome's now in the browser; the channel hands it to every island each tick), so everyone in Emberholm sees the same hour and is rained on and sails on the same wind. Showers are a schedule on that clock (a slot each, started and lasting as a hash of the slot falls), the same to the last bit in both rules. Each island's own clock still runs its crops, labor and contracts; skipping time in the developer panel moves only that.

features.title: Light and atmosphere
features.notes: Soft light without outlines (the toon ramp wrapped into ordinary diffuse light), ambient occlusion worked out from depth at half size, fog that thins with height and glows toward the sun, bloom on what is brighter than white (the sun, lamps and windows at night), Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping and a colour grade. Shadows reach 70 m. Screen effects in one pipeline without EffectComposer.

features.title: The palette, after the reference picture
features.notes: Lush greens with darker woods, pale warm sand, grey-brown rock, light dusty paths, turquoise shallows over a deep blue sea, a clear sky. Every colour the island is painted with lives once per look in src/render/look.ts, so the classic and new looks compare from the same build.

features.title: Textured ground
features.notes: CC0 textures (ambientCG, Poly Haven; CREDITS.md) laid over the seven surfaces, each texture bringing only its detail (its own average colour divided out) so the palette still decides the colours. Steep slopes turn to rock, projected from three sides. Grass repeats at two scales so a meadow shows no tiling.

features.title: Made models for buildings, props, resource nodes and trade packs
features.notes: Generated with Meshy (concept art painted after the reference picture with nano-banana-pro, then meshy-t2.5 low-poly textured models), compressed with gltf-transform (meshopt, WebP), about 60-260 KB each. Each takes the place of the procedural model of the same id once it loads, fitted into the structure's own box from shared/structures.json, so the rules, colliders and server are unchanged. Painted windows glow at night. The ten trade packs too, each fitted into its procedural pack's box with its straps to the carrier's back. The player's cottage, docks, plots and the glider deck keep their procedural models (they are walked into or onto); so do the vehicles' hulls and bodies (seats, oars, wheels and the sealed hulls are fitted to the rules).

features.title: Trees, rocks and cliffs
features.notes: Trees at full size (a 10 m broadleaf of many lumps, a 12 m pine of ragged tiers), shaded darker inside and underneath, with near and far shapes per 128 m chunk; the trunk's foot keeps the collider's width. Blossom trees by the square. Loose rocks become made boulders. Low bushes, some in flower, grow around you on grass and in the woods. Slopes far too steep to walk get big crags set into them (drawing only).

features.title: Sea, sky and horizon
features.notes: The sea darkens with depth, reflects the sky at a glance and sparkles in the sun, and runs on to the true horizon (the sky dome shows the far sea below it). Painted cumulus clouds that never bloom. Other isles stand on the horizon past the edge of the world, hazed blue. The world tree is a hazy giant on the skyline.

features.title: Grain on built things
features.notes: Buildings, vehicles, docks, packs and props still drawn in vertex colours get the grain of what they are made of: warm browns wood, greys stone, the rest a plaster tooth, projected from three sides in world space. Creatures keep their plain colours.

features.title: Quality settings
features.notes: One look; the old toon look (?look=classic) is retired. How much of it is drawn is the quality (src/render/look.ts, GRAPHICS): high on a graphics card; medium on integrated graphics (no occlusion, nearer shadows); low where WebGL is drawn in software (CI) or there is no WebGL2: of the screen effects only the haze and the grade, the frame at three quarters of the window's size, plain ground colours, small shadows that hills don't cast, every tree in its far shape with half the clumps, a 1200 m view, undergrowth and grass nearer, fewer and plainer clouds, no horizon isles, sea glints or grain. ?quality=low|medium|high overrides. In SwiftShader at 1280 x 720 low draws a frame in 285 to 370 ms where the toon look took 235 to 600 and high takes 2.1 to 3.5 s. On an Intel UHD Graphics chip at 1920 x 1080 the square costs 51.6 ms of GPU a frame at high, 33.1 at medium and 14.4 at low (the toon look took 14.6). tests/stress/look.spec.ts shoots each quality at the same places and hours.

features.title: Jelly slimes
features.notes: Slimes are glossy jelly gumdrops (src/render/creatures/jelly.ts): a see-through shell, bright at the rim, with a window gloss and a glint of the sun, what each kind carries showing inside, a soft pool of shadow that shrinks as it hops, and a face whose mood follows what it is doing (winding up, dazed, dying). They play the same clips as the box slimes, so the crowd, the rules and the server never see the difference; the animation library can still show the boxes (Look: Boxes).

features.title: The hero as a made body
features.notes: In the new look the hero is a made model (painted turnaround from Gemini, made and rigged by Meshy, src/render/assets/models/hero.glb) worn on the hero rig: fit.ts measures the rig off the model's skeleton, keeps a joint for each of its spine's bones, collarbones and toes, moves the skin onto our joints, adds a palm and two finger joints to each hand and closes them round what they hold (the grip in front of the palm, not through the hand). It walks and runs as people do: strides, time on the ground and the swinging foot's path measured off Meshy's captured walk and run (gait.ts MADE_STRIDE), its chest, head and free arms swinging as captured (mocap.ts). The rules are unchanged: walk 3.2 m/s is a jog for a body this size.

features.title: Made weapons
features.notes: A sword, club, staff and bow made with Meshy (Poly Haven's free estoc and mace were compared in the game first and read as a rapier and a mace) held where the box hero's were, as long, so swings, trails and reach are unchanged (madeWeapons.ts). Steel and gold give back the hemisphere light's sky and ground colours, so they dim at night; the staff's orb glows; the bow's string is the game's own, drawn back to the hand. Put away, a made body carries the sword and club at the hip and the staff and bow across the back (stow.ts MADE_STOWED). tools/models/weaponprep.mjs paints a metal-roughness map from Meshy's colour-only textures.

features.title: Moves from animation libraries
features.notes: Any of the hero's moves can be its own keyframes or a clip from an animation library, retargeted onto it bone for bone (retarget.ts): each joint's rest lined up with its source bone's, every turn copied, the body following the source's hip joints sized by leg length, the clip's own travel taken off so the rules carry the body and the feet it plants are held. Bone tables for Meshy, Quaternius and Mixamo. moves.ts picks per weapon: the sword plays Quaternius' sword combo and the club its heavy combo (CC0); Meshy's Triple Combo Attack, split at its three strikes, is the other sword set (?swordMoves=keyed|meshy|quaternius). A strike lands on the rules' first active frame at up to 1.5x the clip's pace. The content library shows a clip on the hero beside its source (/dev/library.html#/retarget), and tests/integration/retarget.spec.ts holds every move's clip to within a degree of it; the retarget-animation skill (.claude/skills) says how to bring in another.

features.title: Mini-games at a table, for a stake
features.notes: Walk up to another player on foot and F offers "Challenge <name>": pick the game and the stake (No Stake, or what you can afford), they have 30 s to accept. Accepted, both stakes go into the pot and a round table with two stools is thrown down between you for the whole channel to see (pegs on its board for the lit beacons); you sit at it until the game is over, Escape or Concede gives it up. The winner takes the pot, a draw or a game the server calls off returns each stake, 30 s away forfeits. The server runs it all (world_game/tables.rs, minigames/): a stake sits in the island's `staked` until the game ends, a pot only ever moves between the two islands at the table and both are written in one transaction, an island loaded while no game holds its stake gets it back (a crash or a deploy mid-game loses nothing), and every island write goes through one ordered queue. WORLD_PROTOCOL 6.

features.title: Beacons, the first mini-game
features.notes: A card-and-board game made for Ruina (the user asked for Sequence; we don't recreate existing games, so this is an original one in the same genre). 37 hexes in a hexagon, six island goods on six hexes each and never beside themselves, the Old Beacon in the middle; 48 cards. Play a card to light an unlit hex of its good, two of a kind to light any hex (the Old Beacon too), or swap a card; then draw back to four from the face-up Harbour or the deck. Four of yours in a straight row wins. 40 s a turn (the server plays for you when it runs out; three in a row forfeits).

features.title: Stone and timber before the house
features.notes: Two lessons before "A Place to Call Home": Quill sends you to Brenna at Stonebreak Quarry to quarry stone from the outcrops and cut a Stone Block at the Stonecutter's Table, and she sends you to Hob in Thornwood to chop deadfall and tie a Lumber Bundle at his sawhorse. A gather step counts what a swing gives, not the swings (both rules). The quest marker leads to the nearest ready outcrop or deadfall, the bench that makes a pack, or the site when you carry what it needs; build sites say where each pack they want is made.

features.title: Your portrait from a studio
features.notes: Your face by the health bar and your picture in the character window come from a scene of their own (src/render/studio.ts): you standing at ease, weapon put away, under fixed lights, in the look's own colours; taken again only when your weapon, team or character (or the hero model) changes, not every few seconds from the world. NPC portraits are still taken from the world.

features.title: Lanternwick rebuilt from a village kit: every building one you can walk into
features.notes: The town's buildings are plans of Quaternius' Medieval Village MegaKit (shared/buildings.json): stone and timber-framed townhouses, rowhouses gabled to the street and longhouses, the Lantern & Gull, the Land Registry, the wainwright's workshop, the stable, the shipwright's shed and the trading posts, 18 in Lanternwick where there were 8, lining its roads. Each is walled, floored and stair-stepped by the rules from its plan (doorways open, upper floors and treads as decks, furniture solid), baked for the server; walk in through a door (it swings open), up the stairs to the floor above. Indoors the house is drawn cut open above your storey, its roof still shading the room, lit warm by its hearth, lamps and windows, and the camera looks down into it from within its walls. Rooms are furnished from Quaternius' Fantasy Props MegaKit (beds, tables laid with plates and candles, bookcases, the inn's bar and kegs, the registry's desk and lectern, the workshop's cart and anvil) plus rugs, straw and hearth fires made in code. The whole town is a handful of merged meshes; furniture is drawn only near it.

features.title: Cottages built from the village kit, stage by stage
features.notes: A cottage on a Hearthside plot is the kit's too (plan "cottage", 6 x 8, gabled to the front): its floor, then an open timber frame, then plaster walls with their door and windows, then the tiled roof, chimney and furniture (hearth, bed, chest, a table laid). You walk in and it opens like the town's houses; other players' cottages the same.

features.title: Goblins: the basic goblin and the creature engine
features.notes: The first of the Split-Eye war-band (design/goblins.md), in the training yard (?yard&goblins=6). A creature is data and a body: shared/creatures/goblin.json (its kind, a stab and a stone throw, and a brain in the behaviours' format) and src/render/creatures/goblin/ (a box body until its model is made), run by engine parts any creature can use, in TypeScript and Rust alike: senses (every player as a foe: weapon reach, bow or not, swinging, recovering, casting, guarding, dodging, stunned), a pack step (attack tokens per foe, one more for an opening such as your back or your recovery, ring places just outside your weapon's reach bunched up behind you, courage from health, friends and foes, and where to run), brain acts walk, strike, throw and heal with conditions that take arguments, missiles in flight, and a flinch for blows at or above a kind's poise. One goblin dies to a sword combo and barely scratches you; six wear you down while only three or four strike at once. Against a sword they wait outside its reach and throw stones; against a bow they come right up. Hurt and alone it runs home and drinks its stolen potion out of reach (a blow spills it); hurt in a band it runs to the biggest group. Not online yet: the server runs the same rules but places no goblins.

features.title: The Windspire's waterfall, and the way into Goblin's Dread
features.notes: A spring pool beside the launch deck spills over the lip and falls free down a slot cut in the south-west face into a plunge pool at the foot (recipe `falls`, cut after the tree and rock scatter so nothing else on the island moves). Behind the curtain, 85 m up, a ledge under a hood of rock: you only get there by gliding in (dropping off the summit lands you on the hood). On it the goblins' landing stage, catch nets, a totem, lanterns, cave drawings, and the portal: F takes you into your party's copy of Goblin's Dread. The pools are under half a metre deep in the rules (no wading or swimming yet).

features.title: Goblin's Dread, the first dungeon: its inner grotto
features.notes: An instanced dungeon (content/dungeons/goblinsDread.json): its floors and walls stand round a spot high above the sea north of the island and are solid only in a copy of it (src/sim/zone/dungeon.ts, crates/engine/src/open/dungeon.rs), drawn with the island put away (src/render/open/dungeonView.ts: rock shell, the back of the falls glowing at the south end with the way out, landing stage, lookout with a pot gong, totem, torches, the tunnel north to a goblin barricade). Cave light: no sun, a cool fill and the daylight through the falls. Anyone knocked down or falling out gets up where it's entered. The rest of the lair (the Warren, its three wings, the chief's hall) is the concept art's plan, not built yet.

features.title: Parties
features.notes: Up to five players, as groups in World of Warcraft: anyone not in a party invites someone who isn't either and leads the party made when they accept; in a party only the leader invites, removes someone or hands on the lead; anyone leaves; a party of one is no party; offline members stay in it. Invite by name (any channel or dungeon) or from the players near you in the Party window (O, or the menu's Party button); an invitation asks in a window of its own for a minute. The party frame under your portrait shows the others' health while they're near and where they are when they're not, and the party's copy of a dungeon. Kept in the server's memory (a restart ends parties).

features.title: Dungeon copies (instances)
features.notes: Through a dungeon's portal your party goes into its own copy (someone on their own, into theirs), a game like a channel (ChannelGame with a Copy space) ticked by the same world thread. A copy is kept 30 minutes after the last player leaves it, and whoever comes back within that finds it as they left it; whoever is in a copy but no longer in its party is warned and put out after a minute; a party that forms takes over its leader's copy, and one that breaks up leaves it to whoever was left. A copy holds the dungeon's maxPlayers. Moving between games takes the player out whole, with their connection and island, and their browser hears `space` (WORLD_PROTOCOL 7). Islands in a copy are saved as standing outside its door, so a restart puts you back on the ledge; reconnecting within the half hour puts you back inside.

features.title: The first refactor: one copy of the rules, areas, content as data
features.notes: Planned and reviewed on 2026-11-05 (.plans/refactor/README.md): fourteen phases on branch refactor/first, merged into beta once at the end. Test tiers (unit tests without a browser, integration before beta, stress before a release); dead code out and the toon look retired for quality settings of the new look; an admin menu (admins named in ADMIN_USERS) reaching every developer page and zone; a /find-assets skill; a Rust workspace (crates/engine, crates/server, crates/tools; the server renamed ruina-server); the client in areas with one bridge to the rules and one Content Library page; content in folders, compiled and checked by contentc; the rules in one Rust engine, run natively by the server and as WebAssembly by the browser; content as data (ids in saves and on the wire, spawns, NPCs, weapons, looks); zones as data, the yard and the battlefield as developer zones, and bots as part of the engine; assets streamed and cached for a game far bigger than 64 MB, binaries in Git LFS; the design bible as a knowledge base anyone can read; AGENTS.md rewritten. Done so far: the survey (.plans/refactor/inventory) and the baseline (395 tests pass in 10.8 minutes); binaries in Git LFS; servers that listen on this machine only; the test tiers (npm run check after a change: typecheck, dead code, Rust format and lints, unit tests; a Rust rules file edited and tested in 7 s; the TypeScript-against-Rust checks in 39 s without a browser); dead code out (knip and clippy guard it); the toon look retired for high, medium and low quality settings; the Admin menu (docs/admin.md: admins named in ADMIN_USERS reach Developer Tools, the developer zones and the developer pages, now built into dev/ and served to admins only; the developer commands no longer open to every player on beta); the /find-assets skill; the Rust code in one format, one copy of each rules helper, and a bug fixed in rebuilding everyone's solids after an island is started over.

next: Village, next: the townsfolk at work indoors (Quill behind his desk, an innkeeper at the bar) once quests and travel can lead you through doors; interior walls between rooms; jettied upper storeys, balconies and dormers from the kit; slate roofs; the lighthouse and windmill rebuilt from the kit; sitting on benches and lying in beds.

Goblins, next (design/goblins.md): online at Thornwood (a band at the southern edge, the server placing it, missiles on the wire, a WORLD_PROTOCOL bump); then the grunt made with Meshy beside the best free goblin (bagatir, CC BY 4.0) for the user to pick; then the rest of the war-band (archer, shaman, hobgoblin, lookout, trapper, wolf rider, Chief Gristlecrown), the Split-Eye camp and its quests, with captives to rescue.

Animation, next: other players drawn on our 60-a-second frame clock step in sixtieths above 60 fps; reins on the horse; keep the cape off a staff or bow on the back; a footrest for the hauler's driver; give the townsfolk (src/render/models/villagers.ts) the hero's gait.

Shared world, next: trading-post demand and gathering nodes shared by a channel (the time of day, rain and wind are shared now; these are still each island's own); choosing a channel (to join a friend in another one); others' parked vehicles while they're away.

World server, next: islands in proper tables rather than one document each, if querying them (trading-post history, guild storage) needs it; bandwidth: send other players less often when they are far away.

Skills, next: balance the tree (its numbers are first guesses: a keystone is 8 to 13 points from nothing, Emberholm gives 31 in all); notables and keystones that do new things, not only bigger numbers; life skills (farming, crafting, sailing) that level by use the same way.
Quests, next: Share (the quest log's third button in the prototype), now that there are parties to share with.

After the beta playtest: appearance for characters (they differ only by weapon); steps or a ramp for the western pier, now that a deck too high to step onto is a wall; stamina for sprinting, if wanted; other players' hits sparking on monsters, not only flashing.
Riding along, next: walking a moving ship's deck; the owner seeing (and turning out) who rides with them; vehicles bumping into each other, not only into people.
Travel by road, next: sea lanes for boats; a key to clear the map marker; check the six-metre hauler across the town square.

The look, next: made models for the vehicles' hulls and the trade packs (their seats, oars, rigging, straps and sealed hulls need fitting by hand); the player's cottage as a made model at each build stage; bushes and hedges along the fields; surf around the crags; a graphics setting in the Settings window instead of the automatic guess; the townsfolk as made bodies, playing the same clips; choosing a look in Create Character (skin, hair, outfit dyes); more moves from clips (a block, the roll, hits and a death from Quaternius' free set; the bow, the staff and the whirlwind from Meshy).

Mini-games, next: more games at the same tables (the Rules trait in crates/engine/src/minigames takes any turn-based game for two); a controller in the game window; onlookers opening the board to watch; the table solid and monsters leaving players at a table alone; the challenge prompt winning over a nearby plot or townsperson when you face a player.

Goblin's Dread, next: the level plan from the concept art (the Warren hub; the water, wind and war wings with the jump puzzles; the sunbeam door; the chief's hall and the stolen lighthouse lens), with the goblins from the goblin session; moving platforms (waterwheels, swinging planks); water you can wade and swim in above sea level (the plunge pool, the cistern); a controller button for the Party window; party-only healing and loot.

Refactor, next (.plans/refactor/tracker.md): test tiers (Vitest for the tests that need no browser, a headless harness for the rules tests, integration and stress tiers), then dead code and the toon look, the admin menu and the /find-assets skill, before the Rust workspace and the moves.

questions.q: Should the open world stay the default page?
questions.context: / now opens Emberholm; the old training yard is at /?yard, and the existing tests still use it through ?test.
It paces gathering, crafting and building like ArcheAge, but it was ArcheAge's most resented system. Ours is generous (12 a minute, 1,000 cap). Alternatives: no labor, or labor only for crafting.
Limited open-world land creates land rushes; instanced or phased neighbourhoods remove scarcity but also some of the pride of place.
Pack theft is what made ArcheAge's trade runs exciting. Options: sea only, flagged zones only, or opt-in.

questions.q: How long should crops really take?
questions.context: Prototype timings are minutes. ArcheAge used 10 minutes to days. Longer timers suit a persistent world; shorter suit sessions.
Emberholm, Lanternwick, the Windspire, Charter Seals and the rest are placeholders in the spirit of the world tree theme.

sessions.title: Life on Emberholm
sessions.summary: Researched ArcheAge's vehicles, gliders, boats, pack running, farming and housing, then built them into a new open-world starter isle with its own terrain, sea, day and night, weather, quests, HUD and saving. The combat prototype and battle server were left as they were; all 132 of their tests still pass alongside 39 new ones (171 in all).
points: New default page: the open world, Emberholm. The training yard moved to /?yard (the old specs now open it there).
Gliders with dive, flare, gusts and updrafts; carts, a drifting roadster, a hauler; a rowboat, a wind-driven sloop and a Merchant Cog built on a slipway; donkey and horse.
Trade packs with routes, demand, freshness and contracts; storms that sink small boats and leave their cargo floating.
Scarecrow farms with crops, trees and livestock; gathering; cottages raised from hauled material packs, with a walls-down view inside.
Thirteen starter quests, an open-world HUD and panels, a developer panel (backquote), saving with time passing while away.
Life systems run as commands inside the deterministic sim, ready to move to a server.
Design bible and this tracker created (design/index.html, design/status.json); ArcheAge research notes in design/research/.

A code review of the night's work found nine bugs, all fixed: boats left with the sail up no longer sail off alone; a second whistle brings back the same donkey; the cog design is on sale at Ilsa's; you no longer wade on a pier above deep water; a ride that a storm broke up is cleared; saving while riding puts you back on solid ground; saves from older versions load; quests count work you did before taking them; and a full bag refuses gathering, harvests and rewards instead of destroying them. Five of these (sail, donkey, cog design, quests, full bag) now have regression tests.

sessions.title: Bug reports from inside the game
sessions.summary: Added a way to report bugs while playing: one key records what just happened and what you say about it, and /fix-bugs in Claude Code works through the reports.
points: \ (or both sticks) starts a report with the last 30 seconds already in it; \ again saves it; Backspace twice throws it away. The developer panel has a button too.

A report holds a transcript, voice.wav (whisper-ready), a video, a screenshot with the HUD, frames, console output and errors, game events and commands, the player timeline and inputs, the full state at the press and at the end, and the island save.
The dev server (vite.config.ts, tools/bugReports.ts) writes reports to bugs/ (git-ignored) and only accepts them from the game on this machine.
tools/bugs.mjs lists, summarizes, transcribes (whisper.cpp, if installed) and closes reports; .claude/skills/fix-bugs/SKILL.md is the /fix-bugs routine.
tests/integration/bugreport.spec.ts records a full report with a stand-in microphone and speech recognizer, checks every file, the discard path and the server refusing writes from elsewhere.

sessions.title: Swings land on the hills
sessions.summary: Melee swings did nothing in the open world: the sword, club and staff never hurt the slimes or the practice dummy. Arrows worked.
points: Cause: the swing check skipped any swing with the player more than 2 m up, meant as "in the air". On Emberholm height is measured from the sea, and the meadow and the dummy are 18 m up, so every swing there was skipped.
Fix (src/sim/player/attacks.ts): the check uses your height above the ground under you. In the flat yard that is still just your height, so the rules the Rust server mirrors are unchanged.
On hills a swing also only reaches targets whose feet are within 2 m of yours, the same rule the server uses between fighters, so you cannot hit a slime down a cliff.

The practice dummy's straw burst, when you knock it down, was drawn at a fixed height above the sea, inside the hill under the meadow. It now bursts from the ground under the dummy (src/render/vfx.ts).
New test in tests/integration/world.spec.ts: sword, club and staff swings hurt a slime on the meadow, the sword hurts the dummy, and a slime 3 m down a rock edge is out of reach.

sessions.title: The design bible lives in the source
sessions.summary: The design bible is now a page of the game's source, served by the dev server at /design/, instead of a self-contained snapshot published to claude.ai.
points: design/bible.ts draws everything that comes from data by importing the modules the game runs on: src/content/ (shared/*.json), the tuning, the rules' freshness and climate formulas, and the zone recipe grown by the real generator. The map's relief is shaded in the browser.
Gone: design/build.mjs, design/map.ts and npm run design, and the 400 KB of copied JSON and base64 map they wrote into design/index.html. Change the data or the tracker and the page reloads with it.
design/index.html is now a proper document (without a doctype the dev server showed it in quirks mode) and design/ is type-checked with the rest.
tests/integration/design.spec.ts: every part draws without a console error, the ledger, vehicles, quests and log match the data, the tracker filters work, and the map is the generated island.

sessions.title: Going online: accounts and islands on the server
sessions.summary: Phase 1 of the world server. Emberholm is now played signed in, with your island and build kept in Postgres by the Rust server instead of in the browser, and the whole game builds into one Docker image ready for Railway.
points: Decided: extend the Rust server rather than add a TypeScript one; one shared Emberholm in channels; username-and-password accounts; Postgres, Docker for development, Railway for hosting.

The server now serves everything on one port with axum: /api (health, me, register, login, logout, dev-login), /ws/world and /ws/battle, plus the built game when STATIC_DIR is set. The battlefield can be switched off with --battle off (the Docker image does); ?server=ws://host:port still finds it.

crates/server/migrations/ holds the schema (accounts, sessions, characters), applied when the server starts. A save carries the connection's id, so a window that was taken over can't write over the newer one.

The browser signs in before the island loads (src/app/online.ts), shows who you are and the connection in the corner, keeps playing while it reconnects, and stops when another window takes the character.

npm run up starts Postgres and the server in Docker, so working on the game needs no Rust install. tests/integration/online.spec.ts plays sign-up, sign-in, saving across visits, starting over and the takeover against the real server.

sessions.title: Beta and production
sessions.summary: The game is live on Railway in two environments, beta and production, each fed by a protected branch of the same name through CI/CD.
points: beta takes direct pushes; production only pull requests with CI passing. Both refuse force-pushes and deletion, and beta is now the default branch.
Railway: each environment has the game and its own Postgres 18; Railway's own deploy-on-push from main is gone, so only CI deploys. Local development and CI use Postgres 18 too.
CI plays the whole Playwright suite on Linux against a real server and database, so the battlefield and TS/Rust conformance tests, which need the Rust binaries, run there.
AGENTS.md is the short guide for coding agents (CLAUDE.md points to it). The model gallery and harness pages got a favicon, and the bug-report test reads Windows paths.

sessions.title: The slime pack fight
sessions.summary: Slimes became a pack fight, in five steps each pushed to beta: groundwork for packs on both sides, the slam, bursting and reforming, the rally and gather, and a tuning pass.
points: Brains in shared/behaviours.json choose their next state by condition, can be cut short by interrupts, and wind up, leap and channel. Anything that reaches another actor (calling, pulling, absorbing, slamming) is a request the world carries out after every brain has stepped, in src/sim/actors/step.ts and crates/engine/src/actors.rs alike.

Actors can be spawned and cleared mid-fight and grow into another kind in place; ids wrap at 16 bits skipping ones in use. Home actors respawn only within their ladder's mass budget, and a burst never takes a creature past its cap.

Hit a slime and the pack within 14 m is angry for 15 s: the one you hit calls and the rest rally to it, it gathers them in and grows, and anything in range slams the spot you stood on. Kills burst into slimelets that reform one size up unless you clear them within 6 s.

Drawn: per-size scale in the species crowd, windup, leap, gather and dazed clips, ground rings for slams and gathers, a cast bar on the target plate, splashes for bursting, growing and calling, and a fuse pulse on the pieces. The actor wire entry carries the slam target so the ring shows online too.

The server now steps monsters 60 times a second whatever its tick rate, as the browser does (they ran at a third of the speed on a 20 Hz server), and lands their slams on players with the usual dodge and guard rules.
Tuning: burst pieces only run while you are within 5 m and huddle otherwise, so a group that survives comes back where its pieces are instead of fanning out across the field.

ai-conformance now runs whole packs through both sides (bursts, reforms, a gather, a broken gather) and each has to prove it reached the states it covers; tests/integration/slime-pack.spec.ts plays the fight in the yard, paused so only the test steps it.

sessions.title: Playing together
sessions.summary: Emberholm is shared: friends in the same channel see each other and what each has built, the server owns plot claims and knows the island's ground, and the game is live on Railway in beta and production.
points: crates/server/src/play/channels.rs: channels with a cap, each character's home channel stored; presences relayed 20 times a second; estates (houses, farms, ships) shared and kept while their owner is away; plot claims, first come.

src/net/worldPeers.ts draws everyone else with the same hero and the life view in a new others mode (their farms, house, vehicles, packs and glider, but not the island's townsfolk, nodes or weather a second time). Their houses and farm posts are solid. A plot someone else holds says so and can't be claimed.

server/src/terrain.rs reads the island's height grid baked from the TypeScript generator (tests/conformance/terrain.test.ts keeps it current and compares the two), and the server puts back anyone reported under the ground or off the map.
The developer panel is the server's call: DEV_TOOLS=1 (and development servers) offer it; production doesn't.

CI: tests that need a real GPU (several game windows at once, frame rates, screen capture) are tagged @gpu and run on dev machines, not on GitHub's software-rendering runners; all 17 online battlefield tests pass against the new server with a GPU. --battle off now turns the battlefield off; --bots keeps its meaning.

sessions.title: The server decides
sessions.summary: Emberholm is played on the server: every rule, from walking up a hill to selling a pack, runs there, and the browser only sends what you press and predicts.
points: crates/engine/src/open and crates/engine/src/life: the island's movement and life rules ported from TypeScript, with conformance tests running scripted sessions through both.

crates/server/src/play/mod.rs: a game per channel, 20 ticks a second: players from their inputs (no faster than real time), commands on the input they were given with, the slimes and the dummy, combat on hills, islands saved from the server's own copy.

The browser predicts its own player, vehicles and the clock with the TypeScript (src/net/netPlayer.ts, Life in remote mode) and corrects to each tick; the island it shows is the server's. Commands go to the server and their results come back a round trip later.
The developer panel (give, skip time, teleport) goes through the server too, which only accepts it where it allows the panel.

sessions.title: Moving well
sessions.summary: The hero has elbows, knees and ankles, and every animation was rebuilt on them; fighting, you now strafe, back off, and dodge and flip in any direction.
points: src/render/creatures/heroBody.ts: the rig is two-bone limbs (thigh, boot, foot; sleeve, bracer, hand), a neck, eyes that blink and a cape in two halves. The bow string is two halves meeting at the nock.

src/render/detail/: body.ts (analytic two-bone IK, feet and hands to points in the body's space), gait.ts (stride length and ground time by speed, a heel-to-toe rocker, a backpedal gait played backwards), swings.ts (keyframed swings with footwork), humanoid.ts (every pose, still a pure function of PoseInput so the crowd bakes from it).

src/render/character.ts: a stride clock that shortens strides as you slow, inertial blending between states, feet held where they are planted through turns, stops and starts (with a settling step), trails traced from the blade, the bowstring and arrow following the drawing hand, sub-frame timing on fast screens.
Combat stance in the rules (TS and Rust): faceX / faceZ in the input; the input packets grew a byte (battlefield 16 bytes an input, open world 10) and WORLD_PROTOCOL went to 3.

/dev/animations.html plays every animation with the game's timing (slow motion, any camera, a floor to judge feet by); tests/integration/animation.spec.ts measures planted feet (a centimetre at most moving steadily), floor clearance, joint limits, trails on the blade, the bowstring and the glider grips.

Round two: hits throw the body the way the blow shoves you (the close-up hero keeps the knock's direction while the slide dies away); turning on the spot, planted feet keep pointing the way they were put down and step round one at a time; travelling, the weapon goes to the hip or across the back; the cape takes the wind from the way you go. /dev/animations.html gained films that turn the hero (facing) and hits from four sides.

Round three, after playing it: sitting forward, thighs over the seat's edge and feet on the vehicle's footrest; the vehicle hands the hero what to hold as it moves (vehicles.ts Holds: the steering wheel's rim, the oars' handles, the stirrups); the cart's, roadster's and hauler's wheels turn now, square on their columns and facing the driver (they were tipped back, facing away), and the ship's helm turns the way you steer; short stirrups, so the knees bend round the horse; the glider bar ahead of the chin; the bow drawn to the chin; the sword carried ready; and the weapon out for a fight and put away after it (src/render/detail/stow.ts). /dev/animations.html gained films for putting the weapon away and drawing it, running with it away, and driving the roadster and the hauler; the tests measure hands on what they hold, feet in the stirrups, wheels facing their drivers, and a draw that never jumps or sweeps the ground.

Fixes found on the way: Escape (backing out of a circle) and the button that closes a menu are kept until a rules step has seen them, so a fast screen neither drops them nor lets B slide as it closes the skill panel; the server listens on IPv4 as well as IPv6 on Windows too (socket2, dual-stack), so the battlefield tests run there; on the island you start, and get up after a knock-down, standing on the hill at the spawn rather than inside it (both rules).

sessions.title: Parchment & Timber, the skill book and the skill tree
sessions.summary: The whole UI in the look chosen from three rounds of prototypes, MMO windows docked at the sides, and skills in two parts: a large tree to learn from, with points from quests and milestones, and a book of the skills you use, which level up as you use them.
points: src/ui/theme: the look, the scaled UI (with a size setting), pixel icons for everything and live portraits; src/ui/life/lifeUI.ts redone as docked windows, with a character window and a two-pane quest log.
shared/skilltree.json (laid out by tools/skilltree/gen.mjs): 226 nodes in four disciplines, learned outward through their links; the old skills kept their places and costs.

Skill points are startPoints plus the skillPoints of finished quests and milestones; experience lives with the island, counted by the server online; levels feed the same modifier fold as the tree, in TypeScript and Rust together.
Input: an open window has the controller, the press that closes a window is not also a game press, and the skill book (T, View) and tree (N, a bumper) have their own cursor.

The browser and the server agree on getting better: a place reached counts for each quest by its own reach and height (both rules); a hit trains the weapon that landed it, so an arrow trains its bow and a blast nothing; only a kill is a defeat, not a piece dissolving; a build is held to the points the island has earned.

After the review: the portrait shows your shoulders and the character window all of you again; toasts at the bottom right, smaller; the character window's combo damage and skill points left; the quest log's Abandon and Track on Screen; the merchant's Buyback (Abandon and Buyback in both rules). The skill point amounts stay as they are for now.

sessions.title: The beta playtest
sessions.summary: Twenty things found playing the deployed beta, fixed in four tracks at once: the front door (the name Ruina, a title screen, characters, riding out server updates), the rules (stamina and MP, walking onto platforms, quests heard at once), combat online (smooth slimes, warnings on the ground, hit feedback, the air slash), and the island UI (item menus, the minimap, Title Case, the design system).
points: Front door: a dusk title scene drawn before the code arrives, sign-in on it, an account holds up to six characters (/api/characters, migration 0003, /ws/world?character=), a select screen with the hero live in 3D, and a way back to it from the world. The badge moved under the menu buttons, off the stats line.

Server updates: {t:"updating"}, then every island saved, then close 1012; the page freezes under a card, reconnects, and reloads straight back in when a new build or protocol is out (src/app/resume.ts). F5 also returns straight to the world. tests/integration/update.spec.ts plays it through.

Rules (both languages): stamina and MP (dodges cost stamina, casts MP; WORLD_PROTOCOL 4); decks walked onto up to deckStep and solid when they can't be; a quest stepping on bumps the island's revision, so the NPC window shows it at once rather than 2 s later; the ready toast names the NPC.

Combat online: actors interpolated on a timeline at the render tick (src/net/actorTimeline.ts); circles cut along the terrain's triangles; hits guessed against the server's own rule and played at once, numbers on arrival (src/net/netMonsters.ts); the overhead air chop (AIR_SWINGS).

Island UI: NPC portraits taken from in front of them on a layer of their own; the minimap arrow pointed backwards; quest hand-ins pinned to the minimap's rim; the medallion covered the first line; button text sat high (--cap-nudge); the NPC window 30% taller; room under the minimap; Ctrl+key presses kept from the browser (Ctrl+D bookmarked the page while flaring).
Writing: labels in Title Case everywhere, sentences in sentence case, documented with the rest of the interface at /design/ui.html and checked by tests/integration/ui.spec.ts.
Tests: PW_PORT and TEST_PORT_OFFSET let two checkouts run their suites side by side.

sessions.title: The second beta playtest
sessions.summary: Seventeen things found playing the deployed beta, fixed in four tracks at once: vehicles (friends ride along, riders sit right on hills, no driving with a pack, packs grabbed at once online), animation (weapons out of sight with a pack or travelling, a calm swim, rowing in step, no sea in the boats), the island UI (the drop cap, the mouse back after packing, the farm cart's icon, name plates near you only, one time of day and weather for everyone) and getting about (auto-run, and travel by road from the map).
points: Vehicles: another player's cart or boat offers "Ride with <name>"; the channel seats passengers after everyone has moved and sets them down if the vehicle goes (a host field on the player, the 'ride' command, WORLD_PROTOCOL 5). Everyone else's vehicles are solid (World.movers, both rules). A pack on your back keeps you out of a cart's or boat's seat.

Seats on a tilted vehicle: anchorWorld had pitch the wrong way round, so climbing a hill the driver was drawn a metre ahead of and below the seat. It now turns by roll, pitch and heading as the model is drawn; the ridden vehicle is placed (with a boat's swell) and its wheels and oars moved before the rider is posed in its seat, tilting with it (LifeView.placeRide).

Online: the cart sank into the ground and back on getting in (a server correction eased in under the rider; seat changes snap now). Picking a pack up, loading and unloading one, dropping it, and getting in or out run at once in the browser and again on top of each update until the server has run them; a changed island no longer re-lays the grass or rebuilds every farm plot. ?lag=ms now works in the open world for testing.

Animation: online, every server update replayed the unanswered inputs and counted those frames again, so the clock bodies are drawn by ran two to six times as fast as time, in jerks: the swim on ultraspeed (netPlayer.ts reconcile renumbers the replay). The swim stroke winds its own clock. Rowing: one stroke for both oars, so the hands stay on the handles through turns and backing water. A depth-only seal over each hull's opening keeps the sea out of the boats.
Weapons: out of sight while travelling (vehicles, mounts, glider, swimming) and with a pack on the back except for a strike; only the on-foot places to put it away are left (stow.ts).

UI: the drop cap stands level with the first line's capitals; a window that closes itself after a click (a pack made, a deed used) gives the mouse back to the camera; the farm cart's icon is the cart itself, drawn in tools/icons/bake.mjs; other players' names fade out between 30 and 45 m from you; online the sky follows the server's clock.

Weather: the rain and the wind run on the world's clock online too (Life.worldClock, life.world_clock), so everyone has the same; showers are a schedule on that clock rather than the island's dice, pinned to the last bit in both rules.
Getting about: H or Num Lock auto-runs (cruise in a cart or boat); a click on the map follows the roads there, the route drawn on the map and the minimap (src/sim/zone/roads.ts, src/app/autoWalk.ts).

Tests: riding along and bumping into a parked cart, a pack out of the cart at once 120 ms from the server, everyone sharing the hour, name plates by distance (online.spec.ts); the drop cap and the mouse coming back (ui.spec.ts); travel by road on foot, horseback, cart and roadster (travel.spec.ts); hands on the oars in the real game at 30 and 144 fps, the swim clock, weapons hidden (animation.spec.ts); no sea inside any hull (models.spec.ts); passengers and movers (Rust).

sessions.title: Emberholm after its reference picture
sessions.summary: Overnight, from a painted reference picture of the starter isle: a new look for the whole island (light, palette, textured ground, made models, full-size trees, sea, sky and horizon), the default on its branch, with the classic look kept for comparison and for software WebGL.
